claims.text: Controlled thermomechanical processing can introduce nanoscale precipitation in high-entropy alloys.
Nanoscale precipitation will improve the combined strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance of HEAs.
The improvement arises through enhanced dislocation pinning and crack deflection.
The initial HEA is homogenized and has a single-phase FCC or BCC microstructure.
Cold working followed by aging heat treatment will induce nanoscale precipitation.
The method is applicable to HEAs containing elements that form stable intermetallic phases or precipitates during aging.
Al-, Ti-, or Nb-containing HEAs are examples of alloys capable of forming stable phases or precipitates upon aging.
The processing produces nanoscale precipitates distributed within the matrix.
Nanoscale precipitates obstruct dislocation motion and thereby increase strength.
A small and uniform precipitate distribution reduces stress concentrations.
Reduced stress concentrations enhance ductility and fracture resistance.
The precipitates deflect cracks and thereby improve fracture toughness.
Processing will increase yield strength by approximately 20–50% relative to the homogenized state.
Processing will improve ductility by approximately 5–15% relative to the homogenized state.
Processing will improve fracture toughness by approximately 10–30% relative to the homogenized state.
Processing will cause minimal change in Young’s modulus.
The hypothesis may fail in HEAs lacking elements capable of forming stable nanoscale precipitates.
The hypothesis may fail when processing produces coarse precipitates or excessive grain growth.
The magnitudes of the property changes depend on alloy composition and processing parameters.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement in at least two of strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture toughness would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis says Young’s modulus will be improved, whereas the predicted outcome specifies only a minimal change in Young’s modulus.

The hypothesis predicts improvement of a four-property combination and specifically predicts higher strength, ductility, and toughness, but the falsification rule accepts improvement in any two properties; it could therefore fail to falsify the hypothesis even when one or more central predicted improvements are absent.
